summary:
Adygea stands under the national framework of Russia, where same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection is in force. The propaganda statutes and the extremist designation of the 'international LGBT movement' apply in Adygea as in every other Russian region, and foreigners who breach them face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Russia are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and those publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Adygea is not named in the note as an exception to that assessment, so the elevated-risk finding applies to the republic by default. The note also records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers the North Caucasus republics and flags interior-permission entry regimes, under which travel beyond certain points requires prior authorisation. Visitors to Adygea should therefore expect both the national LGBT-related criminal exposure and an entry regime that is more restrictive than a standard tourist arrival.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or the display of its symbols, of which 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges in connection with the designation, two of them sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or of unknown outcome. On 15 May 2025, three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison, while repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years.
tangentialFactors:
Risk in Adygea tracks identity and visibility rather than orientation alone. The UK Home Office splits its assessment cleanly: LGB people are not generally at real risk solely for sexual orientation, whereas transgender people and publicly active advocates are assessed as likely to face persecution-level treatment. A visitor whose presentation is visibly gender-nonconforming sits in the higher-risk category regardless of the lower headline assessment for lesbian, gay and bisexual travellers.

Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. The 101 convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch by 30 June 2025 are overwhelmingly administrative, but the criminal tail is growing and now reaches publishing workers, a category with no obvious connection to public advocacy. Penalties of up to 12 years for running an extremist organisation and up to four years for repeated display of banned symbols give routine conduct — wearing a pin, sharing an image, holding stock — a criminal dimension that did not exist before the Supreme Court designation.

Government travel guidance from the United States and the United Kingdom now carries explicit warnings directed at LGBT travellers, which is itself a marker of how far official assessments have moved. Those advisories also describe entry-permission requirements for interior travel that a visitor may not anticipate when booking a direct route.
localsOnly:
Residents of Adygea live with the same statutory exposure as Russians elsewhere: no discrimination protection, no legal route to change gender markers, and no access to gender-affirming care since the 2023 ban. Anti-LGBT+ laws affected 139 people across Russia between 2022 and 2024, a figure the UK Home Office uses to gauge the scale of state action against individuals.

Ordinary participation can now be charged as extremism. The 15 May 2025 prosecution of three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 illustrates that employment in print or distribution, not only activism or public expression, carries exposure of up to 12 years. Displaying designated symbols repeatedly is separately punishable by up to four years.

For residents considering leaving, the UK Home Office treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the North Caucasus, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, and assesses that trans people and publicly active advocates are likely to face persecution. That standard governs UK asylum claims and is a relevant consideration for anyone weighing relocation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Adygea-specific enforcement data appears in the available sources. The extremism-conviction figures published by Human Rights Watch are national totals and are not broken down by republic, so the number of prosecutions attributable to Adygea is unresolved.

Whether the interior-permission entry regime described in the US State Department advisory applies to Adygea itself, or only to other North Caucasus republics, is not resolved by the inventory; the note covering the republics and the permission regimes is treated here as a precaution.

The UK Home Office note does not name Adygea as an exception to its higher-risk assessment for the North Caucasus, trans people and public advocates, but neither does it make a republic-specific finding. The inference that the elevated assessment covers Adygea is drawn from that absence of an exception rather than from an express statement.
